description: We are AstroFarmers and our goal is to create a platform that helps farmers decide the best crop rotations for their fields
summary:
Spora is a web app that helps farmers choose crop rotations for the climate they farm in now. Its name is derived from the greek word "σπορά" which means sowing. A farmer draws their field on a satellite map, says what they grow, and answers a few simple questions. Spora then uses open NASA data to show how the weather on that field has changed over 40 years, when the soil lies bare, and how much water the crops need. NASA POWER provides the weather, HLS (Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2) satellite images show the bare months, and NASADEM provides the slope.
Spora compares the farmer’s current rotation with a soil-building option (a cover crop in the longest bare gap) and a water-saving option (a less thirsty crop). It explains the result in plain words: what to do, why, what to watch out for and what to ask an advisor. It also takes into account past pests, diseases and soil conditions on the field.
Spora turns that data into a decision a farmer can act on and leaves the final decision with the farmer.
details:
When the next downpour hits, will your soil be covered?

Weather on a given field is no longer what it was twenty years ago: more hot days, fewer frosts, heavier downpours and longer dry spells. A crop rotation (the order in which crops follow each other on a field) decides how well a farm copes. It decides when the soil is protected or bare, how much water the crops need, and which weather and pest risks hit which crop. NASA already publishes the data to answer these questions for any field, but as gridded files and scientific variables rather than answers a farmer can use. Spora closes that gap.

Local issue: North Rhine-Westphalia

Climate extremes and soil degradation are putting agriculture under pressure worldwide. According to the FAO, one football pitch of soil is eroded every five seconds. North Rhine-Westphalia, where our demo field near Jülich lies, feels this directly. Around 11% of its agricultural land is vulnerable to water erosion every year. The 2021 floods caused an estimated €52 million in damage to farms and agricultural businesses and destroyed about 15,000 hectares of harvest. This is why we built and tested Spora for NRW first: helping farmers keep their soil covered when heavy rain hits protects both the soil and their income.

For each field, Spora gives three things:

  • How the local weather has changed. It compares the last 20 years with the 20 before: hot days, frost, heavy rain, dry spells and yearly rain, each marked as more common, less common or about the same.
  • When the soil is bare. A month-by-month strip of the whole rotation shows when crops cover the soil and when they don’t, and how much of the year’s rain falls on bare soil, which is when soil and nutrients wash away. On the demo field, satellite images confirm the bare months from space, and elevation data adds the slope.
  • Three rotations side by side. What the farmer grows now, a soil-building option and a water-saving option. The best match for the farmer’s priority is marked: save water, build healthier soil, or earn more and feed animals. Each option is explained in plain sentences under “Why choose it”, “Watch out for” and “Ask your advisor”, with the supporting numbers below.

How a farmer uses it

The farmer opens Spora and finds their field by typing a village name or coordinates. They tap the field’s corners on the satellite map to outline it. A short form then asks:

  • which crops they grow in order, with sowing and harvest months (filled in automatically)
  • whether they can irrigate
  • whether the field has had pest or disease problems
  • how they fertilised last season
  • what matters most to them
  • optionally, their soil type, colour and pH

They press “Analyse my field”, and within seconds a window shows how their weather has changed, when their soil is bare, and what to do next. A “Read aloud” button reads the advice in the chosen language. Every step can be undone. An eight-step guide is offered on the first visit and is always available from the “?” button, and outlines drawn at sea or on a lake are flagged at once. Farmers can save their fields with all their answers and results, reopen them later, and export them as a file. Everything is designed for people who rarely use technology: large buttons, short sentences, few numbers.

How it works

  • Field outline: official NRW field-block data (the state register of farm parcels) gives the exact outline, area and land use of the demo field, so the satellite and slope data cover only that field.
  • Weather: NASA POWER daily data since 1981 (temperature, rain, solar radiation, humidity, wind). Spora calculates the water lost to the air with the international FAO-56 standard method and compares two 20-year periods.
  • Bare soil: taken from the crop months the farmer enters. On the demo field it is checked against monthly greenness from NASA HLS satellite images at 30 m resolution.
  • Slope: NASADEM elevation at 30 m, to judge how easily bare soil washes away.
  • Alternatives: the soil-building option places a cover crop only where it can be sown, gets enough warmth to establish, escapes frost and has rain to start. The water-saving option swaps the thirstiest crop for one that fits the same season, ripens in the local warmth and needs at least 20% less water.
  • Field health: rules from agronomy references supplied by our team’s agronomist, Konstantina Dimitrentsi-Chatzivasileiou. Spora avoids cereals following cereals, does not put a cereal cover crop before a cereal, and favours legumes where nitrogen is short. It adds advice such as later autumn sowing after the aphid flight, or resistant varieties on heavy, wet soils.
  • Decisions: there is no hidden score. The farmer’s priority decides which number ranks the options, so every decision can be explained in one sentence. Warnings are counted over the last 20 years and stated as how often they occur, for example “about one year in four”.

The full method, with formulas, validation and scientific references, is available as a PDF from the app’s “How it works” page and in our GitHub repository.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Field-specific: advice is based on the farmer’s own field and the weather it has actually had, not regional averages.
  • Actionable: each option says what to do and when, for example “sow winter rye in September and end it in February, before the sugar beet”.
  • Soil and water: more months of cover means less erosion and nutrient loss; lower water demand means less stress in dry summers.
  • Honest: every statement shows where it comes from, risks and trade-offs are listed, and the advisor questions keep local experts involved. Spora supports the farmer’s judgement and doesn’t replace it.
  • Free and open: built only on open data. No paid services, no sign-up, and saved fields stay on the farmer’s own device.

Spora is aimed at small and medium farms that can’t afford commercial farm-management software or consultants, and at the advisors who work with them.

Scope and next steps

The NASA data and calculations work for any field on Earth. For this demo, the crop knowledge (sowing calendars, cover crops, crop limits and pest rules) has been checked for North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, where our demo field near Jülich lies. Elsewhere, Spora still shows the weather changes and bare-soil months, and asks the farmer to confirm crop suggestions with a local advisor. Next, we plan to:

  • add regions from global datasets (FAO GAEZ crop suitability, global crop calendars and ECOCROP crop limits), with a confidence label per region;
  • calculate satellite cover and slope on demand for any drawn field;
  • add more climate zones and languages;
  • offer optional accounts so fields can be shared with an advisor.

Tools and technologies

  • Back end: Python with FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, Shapely and pyproj. Rasterio and earthaccess for satellite and elevation data.
  • Front end: React and TypeScript with Vite. Leaflet and Geoman for the map and drawing.
  • Hosting: Vercel.
  • Data: NASA POWER, NASA HLS (via LP DAAC and Earthdata), NASADEM, FAO-56, Landwirtschaftskammer NRW crop guidance, NRW field-block data, Natural Earth, OpenStreetMap (place search and water bodies) and Esri World Imagery.

What makes it creative

  • The month strip: one picture that shows the whole rotation, with green for covered and brown for bare.
  • Verbal output: results are written as sentences, with read-aloud, and the numbers follow for those who want them.
  • Farmer knowledge built in: the farmer’s experience of pests, diseases and soil changes the advice, alongside the satellite data.
  • Visible logic: every recommendation can be traced back to a number and a source.

What our team considered

  • The users: farmers with little time and little technology experience, so plain language, three languages, a guided walkthrough, phone support and read-aloud.
  • Honesty about uncertainty: what the data can and can’t know, like area-wide weather, unmodelled soil water, and unchecked markets and machinery.
  • Credibility with agronomists: pest and disease rules, real crop calendars and advisor questions.
  • Privacy: no accounts, data stays on the device.
  • Cost: only free and open data, so any farmer can use it.
